notes: Fictional records, not recovered individuals or an estimate of the excluded cohort. All lipids mmol/L. Population assumption: one rural-active lifestyle regime (100% rural analogue); within-regime diet, activity, infection and medication variation absorbed into stochastic residuals, not separately generated. No population weights or representativeness claim. Recorded F/M is simulated as a binary recorded field, not inferred gender. Main evidence: Lee et al., Am J Hum Biol 2019, DOI 10.1002/ajhb.23199, PMC6435188 version 1, Table 1. Use Maasai subgroup (170 women,161 men) only as an external rural-active analogue: sex-specific age, BMI, TC and HDL means/SDs copied to spec; female probability 170/331. Study was a 2005 rural Kenyan volunteer cross-sectional sample, three ethnicities overall n=1084 with activity data, eligibility >=17, excluding pregnancy and illness, fasting plasma/serum assayed in Denmark. Its subgroup means are marginal unadjusted summaries, not regression estimates. Synthetic adults start at 18. Age truncnorm and BMI truncated lognormal matched to those moments; age cap85, BMI12..55 and age-BMI Gaussian copula r=.20 are assumptions, not published bounds/estimates. TC age slope .015 mmol/L/year and HDL .001/year are magnitude assumptions; Christensen et al. 2016 abstract (PMID26073640; DOI10.3109/03014460.2015.1013987) supports an age increase in plasma cholesterol but not these magnitudes. Association evidence: Soares et al., BMJ Global Health 2019, DOI10.1136/bmjgh-2019-001542, PMC6747887 Table3. Rural Malawi women: TC +.23 (95%CI .19,.26), HDL -.03(-.04,-.02) mmol/L per SD BMI; men: TC +.20(.16,.23), HDL -.03(-.04,-.02). Rural sample n=12096, fasting >=8h; complete-case regression n=4971 women/3548 men. Adjusted age, ethnicity, education, assets, marital status, parity(women), lipid medication, smoking, alcohol, activity, HIV/ART; no diet. Source associations are not causal and are more extensively adjusted than requested analyses. We transport standardized association magnitudes to the synthetic 4.8 kg/m2 SD, rather than claiming conversion using an unavailable source raw BMI SD. This is a consequential explicit transport assumption. Thus conditional TC BMI slopes are .23/4.8 and .20/4.8 mmol/L per kg/m2; HDL -.03/4.8. Assumed no extra confounding remaining beyond age/sex for this synthetic law. Separate F/M slopes yield a pooled age/sex-adjusted projection, not exact source replay. Approx pooled TC slope 8.7 and HDL -1.21 mg/dL per5 kg/m2 using 38.67 mg/dL per mmol/L; these are model implications, not required/fixed sample coefficients. Residual model: TC=HDL+positive non-HDL cholesterol, with independent conditional gamma HDL and non-HDL components and constant component variances. Choose residual variances by subtracting approximate predictor-explained variance from Kenyan marginal variances; copula latent r approximates Pearson r for this subtraction. This is an approximate marginal-variance match, not a fitted covariance matrix. Conditional independence of HDL and non-HDL is a strong unsupported assumption: it implies nonzero positive TC-HDL residual correlation, roughly .32 pooled, because HDL is part of TC. No applicable empirical adjusted residual correlation was found; lipid dependence could differ substantially. This correlation is not a published measurement and should be subjected to sensitivity analysis. Gamma shapes and positive means guarantee positive BMI/lipids without deletion, resampling on lipids, or post-hoc clipping. TC>HDL arises from a component identity, not an eligibility exclusion or row-removal rule. Sampling variation is retained; no orthogonalization or coefficient forcing. Seed determines all records. Source limitations include small external Kenyan subgroup, historic timing, fasting assay differences, Malawi-to-Kenya standardized transport and unspecified target lifestyle composition. Additional retrieved studies were inspected for context, not averaged with these estimands.
